title.narrative: Reduced Emissions from Deforestation (REDD+) in DRC
Stöd för minskade utsläpp av växthusgaser från avskogning (REDD+) i DRK

description.narrative:
The year 2023 demonstrated that the PIREDD Ecuador project had sent many encouraging signals at the end of the project. This indicates potential impact on reducing emissions, deforestation, and forest degradation. However, this overall positive assessment reflects improved results that vary across the program's six components. Two major impacts were expected from the national REDD investment plan:
Reduced emissions and increased removals; and Improved living standards for populations affected by the program. According to the FAO, the PIREDD Ecuador project has reduced deforestation by 0.41% since its launch in 2019. The program's results, which contribute to achieving these impacts, are as follows:
Reduced emissions and increased removals: To reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation while increasing removals, the program focused specifically on three key elements of the national REDD strategy, broken down into technical implementation components. These initiatives aim to reduce the negative impacts of human activity on natural forests, preferably by transferring these activities to savannah regions. Furthermore, the program, developed in advance of the prerequisites, allows for the implementation of activities in planned areas, where established governance structures contribute to the capture, coordination, and orientation of investments by ensuring the coherence, effectiveness, and efficiency of agricultural, forestry, and energy activities. Forests: The program focused on transferring management to communities through Local Community Forest Concessions (CFCL), which require sustainable forest management through the development of Simple Management Plans (PSG). In 2023, a total of 64 communities successfully secured an area of 282,252 hectares of forest for community management under the CLD. Thus, this year, 28 CLD applications were reviewed and validated during a validation workshop in collaboration with the Community Forestry Division, and all obtained legal titles. It is important to note that the Equateur province has secured more community-owned concessions with titles. This would contribute to reducing land conflicts in this area. In addition, four complementary PSG for four CFCL were developed and validated. These actions will restore the functions of these forests, beyond carbon sequestration, timber production, soil and peatland protection, biodiversity preservation, and contribution to ecosystem services (water, habitats, watersheds, etc.).
Agriculture: By 2023, the project was expected to restore savannahs by encouraging sustainable agricultural practices, the use of improved varieties, and agricultural intensification, particularly through agroforestry. The intervention achieved satisfactory results for cash crops such as oil palm and coffee, as well as for fruit trees, spread over an additional 1,300 hectares. This brings the total area planted by the communities to 1,500 hectares. An additional 910 hectares were planted with agroforestry (total achieved: 1,210 hectares). Of a total of 630 hectares dedicated to food crops, 218 hectares were added. Subsequently, the project trained 30 agronomists from the relevant sectors in forest-preserving agricultural methods, as well as 400 farmers and planters. The project also organized 1,001 women into savings and loan associations. This had an impact on the community. Men joined the initiative as the women began to earn income from their economic activities, thus contributing to household needs and children's school fees. Among the activities developed by women is the production and marketing of improved chikwange, a staple food widely consumed in the province and across the country.
Energy: The program aimed to create sustainable sources of fuelwood upstream of the supply chain, outside natural forests, through plantations of exotic and/or fast-growing local forest species in savannah areas.
The project successfully protected 1,989 hectares of protected areas, thereby achieving the target of 8,043 hectares of protected areas. Regarding fuelwood plantations, an additional 488 hectares were created during the reporting period, bringing the reforested area to 909 hectares. These plantations are expected to provide a reliable and sustainable source of fuelwood to beneficiary local communities in the medium and long term. In addition to the areas to be protected, the intervention continued to promote the use of improved stoves, which should reduce the amount of firewood used by households. Since the project began, 6,017 improved stoves have been produced and sold.
By 2023, 2,517 improved stoves had been produced. The project also installed 21 of the 33 carbonization kilns installed to improve production. However, the impact on forest protection is uncertain, as the price of USD 10 per stove was too high for the population, as evidenced by project visits where communities expressed their difficulty in obtaining them.
Improving the living conditions of populations affected by the program: In 2023, the program was able to develop initiatives to the great satisfaction of the population and donors, particularly CAFI and Sweden. The intervention supported the establishment of 15 new Village Savings and Loan Associations (AVEC), representing approximately 135 people in total. Thanks to these solidarity-based savings and loan activities, this helped women and men generate capital. The report indicates that these associations were able to mobilize approximately 1 million Congolese francs, the equivalent of USD 2,750. This demonstrates the economic impact of these initiatives on women, who can thus establish a source of financing.
In forestry: the program contributed to the emergence of 9 forestry micro-enterprises, bringing the total to 131, to exploit Non-Timber Forest Products in Local Communal Forest Areas (CFCL). Payments for Environmental Services (PSE) were paid to at least 873 people in exchange for agricultural activities, land protection, and reforestation. Communities reinvested these funds in community development projects. For example, in Balomba and Lusakani, community projects include the construction of a health center and a makeshift school, as well as the opening of a small business selling pharmaceutical products. This type of support is particularly important given that traveling to Mbandaka from Balomba takes much longer (4 to 5 hours by motorized canoe, twice as long without a motor).
Support for beneficiaries (PSE).
A total of 28,000 households benefited from various forms of support, which should enable them to improve their standard of living.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
